name: Erik Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Erik, 27, a nurse on the stroke rehabilitation ward at Lakeview Hospital. I did a two-year diploma and I've been qualified about a year. I rent a room in a shared house with my friend Jonas, which is cheap, so I've managed to save about a year of living costs and I put money into index funds every month.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you? What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Rehab is slower than the acute wards. People come to us a week or two after a stroke, and our job is helping them wash, dress, eat and walk again, alongside the physios and speech therapists. I love the day someone who couldn't lift a spoon feeds themselves. What wears me out is that I'm still not confident with the clinical bits, like catheters, and I can feel the senior nurses checking my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, the hype was overcooked, but the useful bits are still useful. I'd probably post about the walking exoskeleton we use on the stroke ward, which is a robotic frame that helps people practise walking, because that's real technology helping real people. And I'd tell my mates to stop doom-scrolling about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit bored. I use AI every day, for studying, for drug questions, even to make large-print exercise sheets for stroke patients. I'd keep doing all of that. But I was half hoping for something bigger to ride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on stroke rehab, finish my rehab nursing module, and keep putting money into index funds every month, the way I've done since I started. I'd volunteer to be the ward's go-to person for the exoskeleton and the arm-training robot. Maybe I'd look at a degree top-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly flat, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You make exercise sheets with AI for patients. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a woman on the ward could barely read small print after her stroke. I got the AI to turn the physio's exercises into big, simple pictures with one line each, and she stuck them on her fridge when she went home. That took me ten minutes on my break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even in this flat picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My clinical skills, honestly. I'm still slow putting in catheters and I panicked a bit at my first cardiac arrest call. Money's fine; I've got about a year's costs saved, plus the funds.

say: I'd say the **hype was overcooked**, but useful tools are still useful.
I'd post about our **walking exoskeleton**, real technology helping stroke patients.
think: I'd feel a bit **bored**, since I use AI every day anyway.
I was half hoping for **something bigger** to ride.
do: Finish my **rehab nursing module** on the stroke ward.
Keep putting money into **index funds** every month.
Volunteer as the ward's go-to person for the **exoskeleton**.

fieldNote: He's an **early adopter** who already uses AI daily for patient materials.

With a year saved plus **investments**, money barely registers as a worry.

steps.text: Finish the rehab nursing module on the stroke ward
Keep adding to index funds every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for nurses who are willing to learn, and I'd say it loudly. Let the AI write the care plans and the referrals, and we'll spend the time getting people walking again. I'd be posting tips on which tools actually help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the people who comes out ahead. I already use this stuff, so when the ward gets a new system, I'll be the one showing people. Rehab is hands-on, and robots come into it slowly, as helpers, so my job looks safe for a long while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up straight away to be a digital champion on the stroke ward, and I'd ask the manager, Priya, for training time. I'd start a degree top-up in rehab nursing so I'm not stuck on a diploma when roles get reshuffled. I'd keep investing, and maybe put a bit more into tech funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a bit excited. Like when you get the keys to a new car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put more into tech funds. Isn't that a gamble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small one. I'd keep my year of savings in the bank and only move maybe a tenth of my investments. If AI is changing every job, I'd rather own a little piece of it than just watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on the ward you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our ward clerk, and the older nurses who hate computers. One of them, Bernie, has twenty years on me and still prints the rota. I'd try to help her, but she'd probably tell me to go away.

He'd try to help **older colleagues** but expects to be brushed off.

steps.text: Volunteer as the stroke ward's digital champion for new tools
Start a part-time degree top-up in rehab nursing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough for a lot of people and the government needs to get money to them quickly. At work I'd tell people to learn the tools now, this month, because two years is no time. I'd probably make short videos for colleagues on how to use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be less sure of myself here. The thinking side of my job goes by 2028, which I can handle, but robots that can do hands-on rehab by 2031 are a different story. The nurses who stay will be the ones who run the robots and handle the patients the robots can't, and I'd want to be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go after the robotics side hard: ask to lead on the exoskeleton and any new rehab robots, and contact the companies that make them about clinical trainer jobs. I'd be willing to move city for the right job, because I've got no kids and I rent. I'd keep the year of savings in cash and stop adding to investments for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited in one way, but there's a nervous feeling that I could guess wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you could guess wrong. What would guessing wrong look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Betting everything on the robot side and then the robots don't need a nurse to set them up after all. I'd be thirty-one with a narrow skill set. That's why I'd keep the savings in cash, so a wrong bet doesn't sink me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents if you moved city for this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad drove a forklift for thirty years and lost the job when the warehouse went automatic. He'd say, go where the machines are, son, don't wait for them to come to you. My mum would just ask whether the new place has a good bakery.

I'd make **short videos** showing colleagues how to use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent runway if people start now. I'd be telling everyone at work to take every course the hospital offers. Online I'd be sharing practical stuff, not scary headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is about the best timing for me. I'd do my degree, get good at rehab, and by 2031 I'd be the nurse who knows both the patients and the machines. Robots in 2034 would arrive on a ward where I'm already the person setting them up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree top-up over two years, then try for a clinical specialist role working with rehab robots. I'd keep investing every month. And I'd still help the older nurses, maybe run Friday sessions on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd be the person setting the robots up. What if the hospital doesn't create that job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go where someone has. There are three hospitals and two private rehab clinics in this city, and the robot companies will need nurses who've used the kit. With five years I can be choosy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think the older nurses would make of your Friday sessions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bernie, the oldest nurse on our ward, would come once, say the AI tools are rubbish, and then come back the next week with a question. That's how it went with the new rota app. I'd bring cake, which helps.

steps.text: Complete a part-time degree top-up over two years

Keep investing in index funds every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and people should calm down and plan. I'd tell friends to get into anything that mixes people and technology. Online I'd mostly share interesting robot videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. In ten years I'd have a degree, maybe a master's, and I'd be one of the senior people in rehab who decides how robots get used. The only risk is that I'd get comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree, then look at a master's in rehab or health technology. I'd keep investing and maybe buy a flat in a few years, since I'd have stable work. I'd keep the exoskeleton champion role and grow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited, like a long project with a clear end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said buy a flat. Wouldn't you want to stay free to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years' warning, yes. With ten years' warning, I'd want a flat of my own by thirty. Jonas keeps moving and it's exhausting just watching him pack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any doubts in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the dates are wrong and it comes sooner. So I'd check every six months whether the robot side is moving faster than they said. If it is, I'd switch to the faster plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even I'd be guessing, and a wrong guess in two years is hard to fix. What would help is the hospital being honest early about which roles it plans to keep, and paying for nurses to train on the robots before they arrive, not after. A bit of income support for people moving into new roles would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the patients who'd want a robot. Some of my stroke patients would rather a machine helped them to the toilet than a stranger, because it's less embarrassing. Nobody talks about that side.

He's confident in slow pictures but **less sure** when robots arrive by 2031.
His plan is to become the nurse who **runs the rehab robots**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because a wrong career guess in two years is hard to fix.
